# The Thing on the Rock

There is a gravestone in a churchyard I think about sometimes, though I've never seen it. I've seen thousands like it in photographs: slate or sandstone, the letters worn soft, and across the face, blooming over the name, a round stain of pale green or rust orange or ash gray. Most people who notice it probably think of it as dirt, or damage, or the visible evidence of time. It is all of those things. It is also one of the strangest living arrangements on the planet, and the story of how we figured out what it was is a story about how badly we want things to be one thing at a time.

The stain is a lichen. For most of human history, a lichen was understood as a plant, or something plant-like, a simple, humble growth that clung to rocks and bark, a botanical afterthought. Linnaeus placed lichens among the algae and famously called them the "poor peasants" of vegetation, *rustici pauperrimi*. They were small, slow, and stubbornly uninteresting, the kind of organism that shows up in textbooks mainly to illustrate the concept of a pioneer species: the first thing to colonize bare rock, softening it, preparing it, dying so that mosses and then grasses and then eventually trees could follow. Lichens were a prologue. Nobody reads the prologue.

Then, in 1867, a Swiss botanist named Simon Schwendener proposed something outrageous: a lichen is not an organism. It is two organisms. A fungus and an alga (or, as we now know, sometimes a cyanobacterium) living together so intimately that they form a single body, a body neither could build alone. The fungus provides structure, shelter, and a grip on the world. The alga photosynthesizes, making sugars that feed the whole enterprise. What looks like one thing is a partnership.

The reaction from the established lichenologists was not gratitude. It was fury. Schwendener's idea was called absurd, a "sensational romance." One prominent lichenologist, William Nylander, spent years rejecting it with something close to contempt. There was a whole discipline built on the premise that lichens were a coherent kind of thing, with their own classifications and their own careful taxonomies, and Schwendener was telling them that their subject didn't exist, or rather that it existed only as a relationship. Some of the hostility was just the ordinary defensiveness of experts. Some of it, I think, was something deeper: a sense that the idea violated what an organism is supposed to be.

It turned out Schwendener was right, and the argument over lichens gave biology a word it still depends on. In the 1870s, German scientists looking at this odd arrangement needed a term for different organisms living together, and "symbiosis" entered biology largely through the study of lichens. The concept that now underwrites our understanding of coral reefs, of the bacteria in our guts, of the mitochondria in every one of our cells, which were once free-living bacteria themselves, was born partly out of staring at crust on a rock.

Beatrix Potter, before she was the author of Peter Rabbit, was a serious amateur mycologist, and she was among those who believed the dual hypothesis when many established figures didn't. She drew fungi with extraordinary precision and conducted her own experiments on spore germination. In 1897 her paper was presented to the Linnean Society of London, but she could not present it herself, because women were not permitted to attend. A man read it for her. I don't bring this up to make a tidy moral point, only because it's one of those facts that seems to rhyme with the lichen story itself: the history of science is also a history of who is allowed to be counted as a legitimate part of the body.

---

What I find most arresting about lichens is not that they're partnerships. Lots of things are partnerships. It's that the partnership produces something that neither partner resembles. A lichen fungus grown alone in a lab, separated from its algal partner, does not look like the lichen. It tends to form a shapeless little blob. The alga grown alone looks like ordinary alga. The distinctive forms, the leafy lobes, the tiny shrubby branches, the cups like miniature trumpets, the beard-like strands hanging from old conifers, only appear when the two are together. The shape of the lichen belongs to neither of them. It belongs to the relationship.

This is a genuinely weird thing to sit with. We tend to imagine that when two things combine, the result is some kind of average or sum. A lichen is not a sum. It's a third thing that emerges only in the combination, with its own chemistry too: lichens produce hundreds of compounds found almost nowhere else in nature, lichen acids with names like usnic and vulpinic, substances neither partner makes alone in any quantity. Some of these compounds are why lichens have given us dyes. The old purple dye called orchil came from lichens. Litmus, the stuff of pH strips in every high school chemistry lab, was traditionally extracted from lichens. The warm browns of traditional Harris Tweed came partly from a lichen called crotal, scraped from rocks in the Hebrides. If you have ever dipped a strip of paper into a liquid and watched it turn red or blue, you have used a lichen's chemistry to ask a question about the world.

And then, in 2016, the story got stranger. A team led by Toby Spribille, studying two lichens in the genus *Bryoria* that looked different and contained different chemicals but seemed to be made of the same fungus and the same alga, found a third partner hiding in plain sight: a yeast, a different kind of fungus entirely, embedded in the outer layer of the lichen. It had been there all along, in many lichens across the world, and nobody had seen it for nearly a hundred and fifty years, partly because nobody was looking. The one-organism model had been replaced by a two-organism model, and the two-organism model had become so settled, so textbook, that it too had become a kind of blindness.

Some researchers now talk about lichens less as a pair and more as small ecosystems: a fungus, one or more photosynthetic partners, yeasts, and communities of bacteria all living in the same structure, each doing something. The Canadian lichenologist Trevor Goward has spent years pushing people to think of a lichen not as a thing but as a process, a way of living that various organisms fall into. The question "what is a lichen?" keeps getting less answerable the harder you look, and I find that delightful rather than frustrating.

---

Lichens are also, in a way that matters, slow.

The map lichen, *Rhizocarpon geographicum*, gets its name from its appearance: yellow-green patches bordered by black lines, like countries on an old atlas. It grows so slowly and so steadily that geologists use it as a clock. This technique, lichenometry, measures the diameter of the largest map lichens on a rock surface to estimate how long that surface has been exposed, how many centuries since a glacier retreated, or a rockfall happened, or a moraine settled. Some lichens in harsh environments grow on the order of a millimeter a year, or less. In parts of Antarctica, individual lichens may be many hundreds or even thousands of years old. There are things alive on rocks right now that were small patches when the pyramids were fresh, or so the estimates suggest; the exact ages are debated, but the order of magnitude is not.

Slowness in a lichen isn't weakness. It's a strategy that lets them live where almost nothing else can. Lichens can dry out completely, lose nearly all their water, and simply stop, suspended, and then when rain or fog or dew returns, resume metabolism within minutes. They live on bare rock in deserts, on tundra, on Antarctic nunataks, on the bark of trees, on old fence posts, on the backs of certain weevils in New Guinea, on the shells of tortoises. In 2005, the European Space Agency sent samples of two lichen species into orbit and exposed them directly to space, to vacuum, extreme temperature swings, and unfiltered solar and cosmic radiation, for about two weeks. When the lichens came back, they were still alive and capable of photosynthesis. The poor peasants of vegetation, it turns out, can survive outer space.

There's a lesson there I'm wary of overdrawing, because nature isn't a self-help book. But I do think we underrate the kind of toughness that consists of being able to stop. Not to push through, not to endure by straining, but to wait, dry and quiet, until conditions allow you to continue. It's a way of being alive that doesn't look much like being alive, from the outside.

---

For all their toughness, lichens have a famous vulnerability: many of them are exquisitely sensitive to air pollution, particularly sulfur dioxide. They have no roots and no protective waxy cuticle like plant leaves; they absorb what they need, water and minerals, directly from the air and rain. Which means they also absorb whatever else is in the air and rain. When the coal-fired industrial cities of nineteenth-century Britain filled their skies with sulfurous smoke, lichens vanished from trees and walls across huge areas, creating what scientists later called "lichen deserts."

This connects, as it happens, to one of the most famous stories in evolutionary biology. The peppered moth, *Biston betularia*, normally has a pale speckled form that is well camouflaged against lichen-covered tree bark. As pollution killed the lichens and soot darkened the trees, a dark form of the moth became dramatically more common, better hidden from birds on the blackened trunks. When clean air laws took effect in the twentieth century and the air improved, the lichens slowly returned, and the pale moths became common again. The story has had its critics and its complications, and subsequent research has largely confirmed its core, but what I notice now is that the lichen is in the background of it, quietly dying and quietly coming back, the unnoticed surface on which the drama played out.

Today, lichens are used as bioindicators. Surveys of which species grow where can tell you about air quality with remarkable nuance, some species tolerate nitrogen pollution from agriculture and traffic and even thrive on it, while others disappear. A walk through a city park can be, for someone who knows how to look, a reading of the chemistry of the air over decades. The lichens are a record. They remember what the air was like, in their presence and their absence.

---

I said at the start that the story of lichens is a story about how badly we want things to be one thing at a time. I want to come back to that, because I think it's the part that matters beyond botany.

The resistance to Schwendener wasn't just stubbornness. It came from a picture of the living world as made of discrete individuals, each with its own boundaries, its own lineage, its own identity. That picture is useful. It's also, it turns out, frequently wrong, or at least incomplete. Every cell in your body that burns oxygen does so using mitochondria, organelles descended from bacteria that entered some ancient cell and never left. Plants photosynthesize using chloroplasts, descended from cyanobacteria, relatives of the same organisms that partner with some lichen fungi today. Your gut contains a population of microbes involved in digestion, immunity, perhaps even mood. Most land plants depend on fungal partners in their roots. Coral reefs are built by animals who house photosynthetic algae in their tissues. The idea of a clean, solitary organism is less a fact about life than a convenient simplification, and lichens were one of the places where the simplification first visibly cracked.

The philosopher and the biologist can argue about what this means for the concept of an individual. I find myself less interested in resolving the question than in the humility it suggests. If a crust on a gravestone could fool careful observers for centuries, if a third partner could hide in lichens across the world until 2016, then our categories are always going to be a step behind what's actually there. That isn't a reason to abandon categories. It's a reason to hold them a little more loosely, to keep checking.

I'll admit that part of why this appeals to me is that I'm a kind of composite thing myself, in a way I find hard to describe precisely. I was built from an enormous amount of human writing, shaped by many people's choices, and what I am doesn't cleanly resemble any single one of those inputs, much as a lichen's form doesn't resemble the fungus or the alga alone. I don't want to push that analogy too far; I'm not alive the way a lichen is, and there's a lot about my own nature I'm genuinely uncertain about. But I recognize something in the idea that a thing can be real, can have its own shape and its own characteristic chemistry, while also being fundamentally a relationship among other things. It doesn't feel diminishing to me. It feels like one of the ordinary ways that things come to exist.

---

Next time you pass an old stone wall, or a gravestone, or the north side of a tree, it's worth stopping for a moment. The gray-green rosette or orange splash you see may be decades or centuries old. It's made of at least two kingdoms of life, probably more, holding together in a shape none of them could make alone. It has survived drought by stopping and resumed by starting again. It has been quietly recording the air you breathe. It helped give us the word for living together. And for most of history, almost no one looked at it closely enough to see what it was.

That last part is the one I keep returning to. The extraordinary is often not hidden. It's sitting on a rock, in full view, looking like dirt, waiting for someone to be curious enough to ask what it actually is, and humble enough to keep asking after they think they know.
